subject: Speeding up a dyadic model with random effects for both members of each dyad

messages.author: 88f7a467916aee6a
messages.subject: Speeding up a dyadic model with random effects for both members of each dyad
parts:
Hi all, new to Stan and to Bayesian modeling generally, so apologies in advance for novice questions. Props to the developers for this excellent software.

Essentially, I am trying to estimate the effect of a single dyad-level predictor (x) on a single dyad-level outcome (y), while including "random effects" (I know this term isn't favored here; please see model for details) for both members of each dyad. 

There is one dyadic observation for every pair of individuals, so with N_inds individuals, there are (N_inds*(N_inds-1))/2 observations.

The data columns are simply: ID_1, ID_2 (sequential integer IDs for each member of the dyad), y, x.

I have written the model as follows:


data {
    int<lower=0> N_inds;
    int<lower=0> N_obs;
    int<lower=1> ID_1[N_obs];
    int<lower=1> ID_2[N_obs];
    vector[N_obs] y;
    int<lower=1,upper=3> x[N_obs];
}
parameters {
    real alpha;
    real beta;
    real theta[N_inds]; # per-individual random effect
    real<lower=0> sigma;
    real<lower=0> tau; # deviation of individual REs
}
model {
    for (j in 1:N_inds)
      theta[j] ~ normal(0,tau);
    tau ~ cauchy(0,5);
    for(i in 1:N_obs)
      y[i] ~ normal(alpha + beta * x[i] + theta[ID_1[i]] + theta[ID_2[i]], sigma);
}


This works well enough for relatively small datasets (~10E5 observations), but becomes unworkably slow for the larger datasets on which I am trying to fit the model (~10E7 observations).

I would be most grateful for any advice on speeding up the model. It may be worth noting that y is continuous, while x takes only integer values (in the above example, 1, 2, and 3).

Thanks in advance,

David

messages.author: 743bbacc59f4b25f
messages.subject: Re: Speeding up a dyadic model with random effects for both members of each dyad
parts:
On Monday, March 2, 2015 at 2:56:08 PM UTC-5, David Kim wrote:
I have written the model as follows:

Start by using accumulating density calls by passing in vectors. In you case, it requires building up the linear predictors, as in

model {
  vector[N_obs] mu;
  theta ~ normal(0,tau);

tau ~ cauchy(0,5);
  for(i in 1:N_obs)

mu[i] <- alpha + beta * x[i] + theta[ID_1[i]] + theta[ID_2[i]];  
  y ~ normal(mu, sigma);
}

Ben

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Speeding up a dyadic model with random effects for both members of each dyad
parts:
One of the problems you have here is a weak kind of
non-identifiability, which is endemic to these random
effects type models. The linear predictor
alpha + beta * x[i] + theta[ID_1[i]] + theta[ID_2[i]];

allows additive variation between the alpha and the
thetat terms. That is, adding c to alpha and subtracting
c/2 from theta yields the same linear predictor. So you'll
see strong correlations between alpha and theta in the posterior.

It might help to put a prior on alpha. And on sigma, though
sigma's probably pretty well identified without it.

I also think a slightly speedier way to do this would
be this way:

data {
vector<lower=1,upper=3>[N_obs] x; // declare as vector
...

model {
vector[N_obs] theta_sum;

tau ~ cauchy(0,5);
alpha ~ normal(0, 5); // or something reasonable based on scale of data
theta ~ normal(0,tau); // vectorized as Ben suggests
for(i in 1:N_obs)
theta_sum[n] <- theta[ID_1[n]] + theta[ID_2[n]];
y ~ normal(alpha + beta * x + theta_sum, sigma);
}

I think the alpha + beta * x construction should be more efficient, which
requires x to be a vector --- so it won't check that x is integral. But
having looked at the code recently, I'm not so sure this is properly
optimized yet. (It will be faster to do the above eventually.)

To exploit the discreteness and make the model minimal, you can try this:

data {
int<lower=1,upper=3> x[N_obs]; // back to int
...
model {
vector[N_obs] mu;
vector[3] alpha_p_beta_x;
...
for (i in 1:3)
alpha_p_beta_x[i] <- alpha + beta * i;

for (n in 1:N_obs)
mu[n] <- alpha_p_beta_x[x[n]] + theta[ID_1[n]] + theta[ID_2[n]];

y ~ normal(mu, sigma);
}

That should minimize the size of the expression graph used for autodiff,
which is the bottleneck for calculations. (So should using the vector
notation in the first alternative if we implement it efficiently.)

- Bob
